name: Yoga for posture
lead: Yoga for posture refers to using yoga asanas (physical poses) to build flexibility, strength and alignment with the aim of standing and sitting more upright. People use it to change how they carry themselves: a more open chest, level shoulders and a head stacked over the spine can make a person look taller, broader through the shoulders and more composed, and stretching tight hips, chest and neck muscles is the usual route to that change.

Modern postural yoga developed in the early twentieth century. It was revived in the 1920s by teachers such as Yogendra and Kuvalayananda and spread by students of Tirumalai Krishnamacharya, including B.K.S. Iyengar, whose Light on Yoga (1966) helped popularise it worldwide.[1] A 2016 Ipsos study cited by Wikipedia counted 36.7 million American practitioners.[1]

Evidence is strongest for back pain: reviews cited on Wikipedia, including a 2017 review, report moderate-quality evidence that yoga reduces back pain.[1] Small experimental studies show stress-reduction effects of short yoga sessions.[2] No trial found has tested yoga for changing standing posture or appearance.

chain: Poses stretch tight chest, hip and neck muscles and strengthen the back and core
Spine and shoulders sit in a more upright alignment
angle.text: Practitioners use asanas to loosen the muscles that pull the shoulders and head forward and to strengthen those that hold the spine upright. The hoped-for result is better everyday alignment, which changes apparent height and shoulder line.

paras: Postural yoga is built from asanas held for periods of seconds to minutes, often with attention to breathing. Wikipedia reports that a complete session of asanas and breathing averages about 3.3 METs, a moderate workout, while sun salutation sequences ranged from 2.9 to 7.4 METs and yoga without them averaged 2.9, which is light exercise.[1]

Posture-oriented practice emphasises poses that open the chest and lengthen the front of the hips and neck, with core and back work to hold the spine upright. Postural patterns commonly discussed in this context include a head carried ahead of the shoulders and a rounded upper back. Wikipedia describes forward head posture as a head that sits ahead of the shoulders with a hunched upper back, common in people who spend long hours at screens.[7]

Wikipedia's article on asana describes an asana as a body posture, first a general term for a sitting meditation pose and later extended in hatha yoga and modern yoga to any position; the Yoga Sutras describe it as a steady and comfortable posture.[9] Families of postures include seated, standing, balancing, inverted, reclining, backbend and twist poses, with standing poses such as the triangle pose becoming common in the twentieth century.[9]

For posture goals, practitioners tend to draw on standing poses that stack the spine over the pelvis, backbends and chest openers that counter a rounded upper back, and seated or reclining poses that lengthen the hips and neck. Iyengar's Light on Yoga (1966) covers about 200 asanas and describes them as producing steadiness, agility and endurance.[9]

Older yoga traditions were not centred on postures. Wikipedia states that Patanjali's Yoga Sutras defined asana as steady and comfortable, and that Hatha yoga from about 1100 used few, mostly seated asanas held for long periods.[1] Posture-based yoga was revived in the 1920s: Yogendra brought asanas to the United States in 1919, and the Rajah of Aundh popularised the sun salutation in the 1920s.[1] Kuvalayananda founded the research centre Kaivalyadhama in 1924.[1]

Krishnamacharya in Mysore combined Hatha yoga with wrestling exercises and Western gymnastics from the 1930s to the 1950s, and his students shaped the main modern styles: Pattabhi Jois created Ashtanga Vinyasa, B.K.S. Iyengar founded Iyengar yoga and published Light on Yoga in 1966, and Indra Devi taught celebrities in Hollywood.[1] Wikipedia notes that Eugen Sandow's 1905 visit to India influenced Indian physical culture, and that European physical culture shaped modern yoga.[1]

Historian William Broad argues that scientific health claims for yoga began as Hindu nationalist posturing, and Kuvalayananda reportedly found no evidence for his claims about shoulderstand and the endocrine glands.[1]

sections.h: Use in lifting and fitness communities
paras: Yoga turns up in lifting forums mainly as mobility and stretching work alongside training. A T Nation poster in 2022 described slouched desk posture while working on shoulder mechanics for pressing, and another in 2019 wrote that a yoga mat had mostly become a place to stretch rather than to do elaborate poses.[10][11] A 2018 thread on 'woowoo' topics included an account of a long kriya yoga and chanting practice.[12]

Wikipedia describes yoga becoming a global commodity from the 1960s and 1970s, with Lilias Folan's television show running from 1970 to 1999, Yoga Journal founded in 1975, and September designated National Yoga Month in the United States in 2008. It reports a 2016 Ipsos figure of 36.7 million US practitioners, 72 percent of them women, and a US business worth $16 billion, with athleisure clothing worth $35 billion in 2014.[1] The first International Day of Yoga was held on 21 June 2015.[1]

A 2012 study of 20 office workers compared 15 minutes of chair-based yoga postures and guided meditation with usual work; both reduced perceived stress compared with control.[2] A 2017 anatomical study examined core muscle activation in different yogic postures.[3] A 2023 meta-analysis examined yoga and pulmonary function in asthma.[4]

Wikipedia cites a systematic review of six studies finding Iyengar yoga effective, at least short term, for neck and low back pain, and a 2017 review finding moderate-quality evidence for reduced back pain; a 2014 report called yoga extremely understudied.[1] Reviews cited there also describe benefits for depression and for stress and anxiety, with calls for more rigorous trials.[1] No studies found measuring change in postural alignment or appearance.

Wikipedia's asana article cites studies suggesting improvements in flexibility, strength and balance and reduced stress, and notes that asanas have been studied for conditions including asthma and diabetes.[9]

Case reports describe progression of glaucomatous optic neuropathy and visual field loss in patients who practised the Sirsasana (headstand) daily for years, with intraocular pressure rising significantly in the head-down position.[5][6]

A cross-sectional survey of 2,620 yoga asana participants, mostly aged 31 to 60 and 84 percent female, asked about yoga-related injury and reported that the risk had been poorly characterised in the literature.[8]

card.summary: Postural yoga used for mobility and alignment; some evidence for back pain and stress, little direct testing on posture or looks.
card.note: Inverted poses such as headstand have been linked in case reports to raised eye pressure and glaucoma progression.

quick.overview:
Modern postural yoga combines stretches, strength holds and breathing and is widely practised as exercise. Posture and mobility communities recommend it for flexibility and body awareness.

Reviews summarised on Wikipedia report moderate-quality evidence that yoga reduces back pain, and small studies report stress reduction. The sources found include no controlled trial of yoga changing standing posture or visible appearance.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say holding stretched and supported positions improves flexibility, strength and body awareness. One 2017 study mapped core muscle activation across different yoga postures, giving a muscular basis for strength claims.
quick.risks: Case reports describe glaucomatous optic nerve damage progressing in people who regularly practised the headstand, with eye pressure rising in the head-down position. Wikipedia's overview of yoga as exercise cites health claims but notes the field is understudied.
